quote: Als erläuterndes Beispiel diene das Problem: Gesucht wird ein binäres Formenbüschel, dessen Funktionaldeterminante gegeben ist.
english: As an illustrative example, let the following problem serve: a binary pencil of forms is sought whose functional determinant is given.
topic: Applying the concept of a full system of forms to algebraic problems (systems of polynomial equations), illustrated by the problem of finding a binary pencil of forms with a given functional determinant, followed by the start of a question about full invariant systems.

triage.modern_statement: Given a binary form F(x,y) of degree 2n−2, find all pencils ⟨f,g⟩ of binary forms of degree n whose Jacobian f_x g_y − f_y g_x is proportional to F. Changing the basis of the pencil only multiplies the Jacobian by a constant, so this is the inverse problem for the Wronski map. That map sends the Grassmannian G(2, n+1) of 2-dimensional subspaces of degree-n polynomials to P^{2n−2}, taking each pencil to its Wronskian, which is the dehomogenized Jacobian. Put another way: find the rational functions f/g of degree n with prescribed critical points, counted up to Möbius transformations. The questions are whether solutions exist, how many there are (the degree of the Wronski map), and how to construct them. In the notebook, Hilbert uses the problem as an example of applying the 'full system of forms' (volles Formensystem) idea to systems of polynomial equations.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert published on this exact problem himself. His note 'Über die Büschel von binären Formen mit der nämlichen Funktionaldeterminante' was presented at the Leipzig Academy session of 24 October 1887 (Berichte der Kgl. Sächs. Ges. d. Wiss., math.-phys. Kl., Bd. 39). It also appears, apparently, as 'Über Büschel von binären Formen mit vorgeschriebener Funktionaldeterminante' in his Gesammelte Abhandlungen; its summary starts with a count of essential constants (2ν−2). The modern enumerative answer is that a generic F has C_{n−1} = (1/n)·binom(2n−2, n−1) such pencils, a Catalan number. L. R. Goldberg gave this in 'Catalan numbers and branched coverings by the Riemann sphere', Adv. Math. 85 (1991) 129–144. It also follows from Schubert calculus, since it is the degree of G(2, n+1). For the real case, A. Eremenko and A. Gabrielov computed degrees of real Wronski maps (Discrete Comput. Geom. 28, 2002). They also proved that if all critical points are real, then all the pencils are real (Ann. Math. 2002; elementary proof arXiv:math/0512370), which is the n=2 case of the B. and M. Shapiro conjecture.

evidence.claim: Hilbert presented 'Über die Büschel von binären Formen mit der nämlichen Funktionaldeterminante' at the math.-phys. class session of the Royal Saxon Society of Sciences in Leipzig on 24 October 1887.

Springer has a Hilbert chapter titled 'Über Büschel von binären Formen mit vorgeschriebener Funktionaldeterminante' (on pencils of binary forms with a prescribed functional determinant); its summary starts with a count of 2ν−2 essential constants.

Goldberg's paper 'Catalan numbers and branched coverings by the Riemann sphere' (Adv. Math. 85, 1991) shows that the number of rational functions with given generic critical points, counted up to equivalence, is a Catalan number.

Eremenko and Gabrielov study the map that sends vectors of polynomials to their Wronski determinants, which they call the Wronski map (a projection of a Grassmannian), and compute the degrees of its real versions.
If the 2d−2 critical points are real, all the codimension-2 subspaces (pencils), whose number is the d-th Catalan number, are real. This is the B. and M. Shapiro conjecture for rational functions.
For a polynomial pencil, changing the basis multiplies the Wronskian by a nonzero constant, and the Wronskians are polynomials of degree at most 2n−2.

triage.why: The note matches the subject and title of Hilbert's own 1887 Leipzig paper, so Hilbert treated the problem himself in print. The notebook entry reuses it as an example for the full-system-of-forms method. The modern view is the Wronski map for G(2, n+1): the generic count is the Catalan number (Goldberg 1991), and the real version was settled by Eremenko and Gabrielov (2002). It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. Wronski maps and real Schubert calculus are still studied, but the specific question in the note is settled. I could not open the text of Hilbert's 1887 paper, so I can't confirm exactly how far it went (for example, whether it gave the full count). Search limits also stopped me from checking the Catalan count wording and the B. and M. Shapiro conjecture extension beyond the abstracts.
